title: Regional routing, capacity planning & KV-cache handoff (design review)
summary: Architectural discussion about multi-region routing policies, capacity thresholds and automated failover. Key focus: smooth KV cache handoff during cross-region failover, routing policy priorities (latency vs cost), and operational playbooks for DR. Action: run sustained QPS benchmark, provide DR checklist and draft routing policy configs.
topics: KV cache handoff and prefix caching
batching and quantization tradeoffs for DR replicas
action_items: Alex Turner | Send initial routing policy YAML + example failover priority list | 2025-08-25
Priya Nair | Share KV-cache handoff notes and code snippet (consistent-hash approach) | 2025-08-26
Omar Ruiz | Provide target 95th latency SLOs and current QPS by region | 2025-08-24
Lina Chen | Schedule pilot window and list of subnets/VPC peering details | 2025-08-28
next_steps: Redwood to run a 6-region QPS benchmark with two model variants (8-bit quantized and fp16) and share results
Customer to finalise DR stakeholders and emergency contact list
Schedule follow-up POC scoping call to align SLA/comms
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Turner: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, we'll, uh, kick off. Alex from Redwood here, AE on the account, and Priya, SE, will drive the technical bits.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Hi all, Priya Nair. I put the agenda in the calendar note: routing policy, cache handoff, capacity headroom, and playbook. We'll try to be concrete.
[00:34] Omar Ruiz: Thanks. From NorthStar side — Omar — we have SRE and SecOps here, Lina and Mateo. Our immediate ask: we need a failover design that doesn't cause a flash of latency and minimizes cold-start token cost during DR.
[00:50] Lina Chen: Also need to keep data inside EU for GDPR, so routing needs to honor residency where possible but still failover when capacity is gone.
[01:06] Alex Turner: Noted. Quick poll: how many regions do you want active versus passive?
[01:12] Sana Rao: We're thinking active-active for US and EU, APAC passive for now.
[01:22] Priya Nair: That's helpful. For active-active we recommend sticky routing per-user session to keep KV-cache hits high — but we'll talk through handoff patterns.
[01:34] Mateo Alvarez: Can you describe what you mean by handoff? Like how does a KV cache move between regions?
[01:42] Priya Nair: Sure. Two patterns: prefix-level cache replication (proactive sync) or on-demand handoff where you accept a few miss penalties and rewarm. Prefix replication is heavier on network and consistency; on-demand is simpler but causes transient latency.
[02:02] Alex Turner: Right — and for large models the KV cache size matters. We typically recommend per-user prefix caching up to N tokens and gracefully evict.
[02:15] Lina Chen: Any guidance for eviction thresholds? We have GPU memory limits in our Dedicated pools.
[02:22] Priya Nair: Set soft limits at around 60-70% of KV cache per-GPU to leave room for burst. Hard cap at 85% to avoid OOM during batch spikes.
[02:34] Omar Ruiz: What about consistent hashing? Could we use ring-based sharding to route sessions to same replica across regions?
[02:44] Priya Nair: You can — consistent hashing with virtual nodes helps maintain locality. But cross-region consistent hashing requires either routing layer awareness or a global coordinator. That's a complexity tradeoff.
[02:58] Alex Turner: One practical approach we've seen: maintain primary->secondary mapping per-tenant in control plane. Primary region handles sticky sessions; secondary is in pipeline for takeover.
[03:12] Mateo Alvarez: Ok, and during failover — what's the safe way to drain in-flight requests?
[03:18] Priya Nair: Drain at the edge: new requests get routed to other region while in-flight completes. For streaming responses you may need application-level resume tokens. There's also a short lived duplication approach — run both until caches sync then cutover.
[03:34] Lina Chen: Duplication sounds expensive. Latency spike risk?
[03:38] Priya Nair: Yes, duplication doubles cost temporarily. We usually recommend duplication only for critical tenants during planned failover windows.
[03:48] Alex Turner: I'll add cost estimates to the routing policy doc.
[03:52] Sana Rao: Can Redwood's routing policy be driven by SLOs like 95th latency threshold and also capacity thresholds?
[04:00] Priya Nair: Yes — policy engine supports multi-key priorities: prefer lowest-latency region but degrade to lowest-cost region if latency SLO breached or capacity saturates. You can also configure region-blacklist if regulatory outage.
[04:14] Omar Ruiz: Good. We want failover to prefer EU for EU users until EU capacity > 85% then fail to US, but in emergency fail to APAC.
[04:26] Priya Nair: You can express that as ordered priority lists plus capacity-based triggers. We'll share sample YAML.
[04:34] Alex Turner: Let's pivot to KV cache handoff specifics — Priya?
[04:38] Priya Nair: Ok. In our runtime we support prefix caching (client or runtime-side). For cross-region failover, we have three handoff flows: 1) cold handoff — accept miss and rewarm, 2) remote fetch — ask primary region for KV segments over an authenticated channel (adds latency), 3) proactive replication — stream checkpoints to secondaries.
[05:00] Omar Ruiz: Remote fetch with auth sounds promising if it's only a handful of tokens. How do you secure that?
[05:06] Priya Nair: TLS + mTLS between regional clusters, with mutual certs or KMS-backed ephemeral creds. We log fetches for audit. There are also ACLs per-tenant.
[05:16] Mateo Alvarez: Any SOC2 implications? We need audit trail and no plaintext outside EU.
[05:22] Alex Turner: We can configure replication to stop for EU tenants — mark them residency-locked so only local region used. We'll add audit log details to the security appendix.
[05:34] Lina Chen: What about batching during failover? If many sessions move simultaneously, token-level batching could spike CPU/GPU.
[05:44] Priya Nair: Right. We have adaptive batching: when overload detected, we reduce max batch size and enforce smaller latency SLOs. Also we prefer request-priority qps shaping to protect control traffic.
[05:58] Omar Ruiz: How does quantization play into failover? We have two model builds: fp16 primary and 8-bit quantized fallback.
[06:08] Priya Nair: Using a quantized fallback helps capacity — you get 2-3x throughput at cost of slight quality loss. Auto-fallback based on capacity thresholds is supported, but you should do evals first.
[06:20] Alex Turner: We'll run quality regressions during the POC. Priya, can you demo how the routing engine flips model variants?
[06:27] Priya Nair: Yes — policy has a model-variant map: if region A saturates, switch to quantized variant in region B or same region. It's an atomic pointer swap in runtime.
[06:36] Sana Rao: Any risk of tokenization differences between fp16 and quant?
[06:41] Priya Nair: Tokenization is the same; differences come from numerical precision but shouldn't change token boundaries. But outputs might vary.
[06:48] Omar Ruiz: For DR playbook, what are the recommended runbook steps?
[06:52] Priya Nair: High-level: 1) Detect (metrics + control-plane alerts), 2) Notify (ops pager & stakeholders), 3) Quarantine traffic (soft failover), 4) Promote secondary (attach model and warm caches), 5) Validate (synthetic probes), 6) Reroute permanently or rollback.
[07:08] Lina Chen: How long is step 4 — promote secondary — expected to take?
[07:12] Priya Nair: Depends on rewarm strategy. Cold rewarm ~ minutes to tens of minutes; remote fetch could be 200-700ms per user to rehydrate; proactive replication provides near-instant.
[07:26] Alex Turner: For NorthStar, with medium session stickiness, remote fetch seems a good tradeoff.
[07:33] Mateo Alvarez: We don't want inter-region data copies for EU tenants. So remote fetch must be disabled for those.
[07:40] Priya Nair: We'll annotate tenants as residency-locked. For those, only local region is allowed — which implies under capacity pressure, we might return 503 or degraded modes.
[07:52] Omar Ruiz: Are there graceful degradation modes? Like returning shorter completions or cost-aware truncation?
[07:58] Priya Nair: Yes — we support response-slimming: reduce max tokens, beam-size, and fall back to simpler models. That reduces compute footprint.
[08:10] Alex Turner: Ok let's discuss testing: what should the POC bench look like?
[08:15] Priya Nair: We propose: steady-state baseline, 2x traffic spike, region outage simulation (kill control plane in EU), and cross-region handoff, all with telemetry on KV hit rates, 95/99 latencies, and token cost.
[08:31] Omar Ruiz: Can Redwood run that in our dedicated test account?
[08:34] Alex Turner: Yes, we can spin up a Dedicated pilot and run the benchmark. We'll need VPC peering or private link details.
[08:42] Lina Chen: We'll share peering info as an action item.
[08:46] Priya Nair: On metrics: watch KV cache hit rate, rewarm traffic volume, and per-request token compute time. Also track batching efficiency — average batch size and queue latency.
[08:58] Mateo Alvarez: If we throttle to preserve latency, we might reduce average batch size — hurting cost. Any heuristics?
[09:06] Priya Nair: Heuristics: prefer lower latency SLOs for interactive workloads — sacrifice batching. For background/async calls, increase batch sizes aggressively. You can tag routes accordingly.
[09:18] Alex Turner: We should put recommended route tags in the YAML.
[09:22] Sana Rao: Let's touch on private deployments — we may want Redwood private in our EU data center. How does the routing differ?
[09:30] Priya Nair: Private deployments run local control plane with optional federation to Redwood's central control for metrics. Routing policies can be local or federated; with strict residency you run fully local and central plane acts as admin only.
[09:44] Omar Ruiz: For private, do we still get automatic failover to other private sites?
[09:48] Priya Nair: If you federate your private sites and allow cross-site network peering, yes. Otherwise you'd need manual switch. We can do hybrid: automated within your private network, manual to cross-cloud.
[10:00] Lina Chen: Security: KMS integration for ephemeral certs, HSM?
[10:04] Alex Turner: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and can do HSM-backed keys in Private. We'll include a security checklist.
[10:12] Mateo Alvarez: For the actual failover communication channels, what's the protocol used for KV fetch?
[10:18] Priya Nair: We use gRPC with flow-control to avoid head-of-line; we also chunk large KV windows to avoid single big RTTs.
[10:28] Omar Ruiz: Are there known edge-cases — e.g., split-brain if control plane partitioned?
[10:34] Priya Nair: Yes. We recommend leader election with quorum and conservative default: if uncertain, do not promote secondaries automatically; instead put in read-only mode and alert operators.
[10:46] Alex Turner: Let's show a simple example of the routing policy — Priya, walk the YAML.
[10:50] Priya Nair: Sure. (screen share audio) Example: priorities: {eu-primary, us-secondary, apac-fallback}, capacity_trigger: {cpu>85% or gpus_util>80%}, model_variant_switch: on_threshold, residency_exceptions: [tenant tags]. We'll send the full snippet.
[11:10] Sana Rao: Please include the exact metric names — our SRE team needs them.
[11:14] Priya Nair: Absolutely. We'll include metric namespaces and sample Grafana dashboards.
[11:20] Omar Ruiz: How does the control plane push new policy without blipping traffic?
[11:26] Priya Nair: Policy pushes are transactional; we push to edge proxies with a staged rollout and can canary to a subset of tenants before global.
[11:36] Lina Chen: Is there a circuit-breaker we can set per-tenant?
[11:40] Priya Nair: Yes, per-route circuit breakers with fail-open or fail-close semantics.
[11:44] Mateo Alvarez: For our compliance team — can we get a runbook that ties into our SOC2 incident response?
[11:50] Alex Turner: We'll add a SOC2 appendix to the playbook with contact points and log retention details.
[11:58] Omar Ruiz: Any quick wins to reduce failover effort?
[12:02] Priya Nair: Tagging routes by sensitivity, enabling small proactive replication window for hot prefixes, and setting early warning alerts at 70% not 85% so you have room to act.
[12:16] Sana Rao: That seems reasonable.
[12:18] Alex Turner: Ok — questions from the customer side?
[12:20] Lina Chen: One more — what about billing/chargeback during cross-region duplication? How is cost attributed?
[12:28] Alex Turner: We can produce cost reports per-tenant per-region. Duplication will show as additional usage and we will tag it. For Dedicated, surcharges may apply for extra GPU hours.
[12:40] Omar Ruiz: Speaking of surcharges, how do we estimate the cost of duplication for a 1,000 concurrent user black swan event?
[12:48] Priya Nair: Back-of-envelope: duplication doubles active GPU hours for the duplicated tenants. For 1k concurrent, depending on model size, might be tens to low hundreds of GPU-hours — we'll produce a more precise estimate in the follow-up.
[13:04] Alex Turner: We'll run a modeled estimate and include it in the YAML doc.
[13:10] (brief cross-talk)
[13:20] Priya Nair: Quick callout on KV cache sync: chunking strategy matters. If you transfer whole KV per session you get network spikes; instead transfer N most-recent segments and let runtime fetch rest lazily.
[13:34] Mateo Alvarez: How many segments are typical?
[13:38] Priya Nair: Depends on model context window, but often 3-5 most-recent segments buys you good perf.
[13:46] Omar Ruiz: For warm-up scripting, can we use synthetic prompts to pre-warm caches?
[13:52] Priya Nair: Yes, synthetic traffic is effective — but ensure it's representative to avoid mismatched cache content.
[13:58] Lina Chen: Ok, timeline — when can we expect the docs and sample configs?
[14:02] Alex Turner: We'll deliver routing YAML, KV handoff notes, and a DR checklist by Aug 25. Priya will add code snippets.
[14:12] Sana Rao: Can we also get the benchmark plan?
[14:14] Priya Nair: Yes — benchmark plan and telemetry dashboard will be included.
[14:20] Omar Ruiz: Anything else?
[14:22] Mateo Alvarez: I'd like an example of a failover incident timeline with timestamps so we can practice the runbook.
[14:28] Priya Nair: We'll draft a sample timeline: detection at t0, notify at t0+1m, soft failover at t0+3m, validate at t0+6m, full promotion at t0+10m, rollback criteria spelled out.
[14:44] Alex Turner: Great. Last logistics: follow-up POC scoping call next Tues?
[14:50] Omar Ruiz: Works for us.
[14:52] Alex Turner: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and next steps.
[14:56] (meeting ends, informal chatter)
crm_notes: SE product deep dive; customer cares about EU residency and minimal latency spike on failover. AE to own cost estimates. Technical owner from NorthStar (Omar) will provide SLOs.
